newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien relentlessly grilled in debate.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien relentlessly grilled in debate.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien came under merciless criticism on Monday night from all his rivals during the sole English-language debate before the June 2 federal election.

As the incumbent and the undisputed leader in national polls, he proved a juicy target for the leaders of the other four main parties contesting the election, whether separatist or federalist, right-wing or socialist.

The 2-1/2-hour debate was free-wheeling, even raucous, as the leaders tore into each other, but especially into Chretien, on issues ranging from health care cuts to the near victory by Quebec separatists in a referendum.
"You almost blew it, sir," Reform Party leader Preston Manning declared, referring to the October 1995 Quebec vote, when Chretien told Canadians not to worry. "You do not deserve a second chance."

Every leader pointed out that 3-1/2 years ago, during the last election, Chretien had guaranteed in the last debate that he would not cut health spending -- and then cut $7 billion Canadian ($5 billion U.S.) from health and social transfers to the provinces.

Chretien pointed out that his government had pledged to restore some of the cuts -- on the second day of the campaign -- because the light was visible at the end of the tunnel after years of slashing budget cuts.
"The light he saw at the end of the tunnel was the white of the eyes of the Canadian voter," Conservative Party leader Jean Charest declared.

Leftist New Democratic Party leader Alexa McDonough charged that Chretien's Liberals had broken promises to scrap the hated federal Goods and Service Tax, not to cut health spending, and to make jobs the top priority.

Gilles Duceppe of the Bloc Quebecois declared Quebec would soon be a sovereign country, but he spent much of his time attacking the government's slow progress in reducing unemployment insurance premia.
Even one of the television reporters posing questions was withering.
"You assured us before the last referendum that if we all shut up everything would be just fine, and then you almost lost the country," blurted CTV reporter Craig Oliver.
The 63-year-old leader, not speaking in his native French language, was once or twice speechless but did try to launch counter-attacks -- but found himself fighting a four-front war.

Addressing McDonough's goals for more spending, he pointed out it had been necessary to restore Canada's international financial position: "You won't have any social programmes in Canada if you have a bankrupt nation."
He said his vision for keeping Canada together was to work on problems one at a time.

Chretien went into the debate with a lead of at least 20 points in the polls, including a crushing majority that appeared likely to give him a near sweep in the prize province of Ontario, with 103 of the 301 seats in the House of Commons.

Chretien has been criticised in central Canada for calling the election in the middle of flooding in Manitoba, blasted on the left for spending cuts and pressured by Conservatives and Reform for tax cuts.
Pollsters caution that Canadian voters have been showing increasing volatility in recent years. Another debate, in French, was scheduled for Tuesday night.
